findings.title: Every re-scrape deletes the listing's price history
findings.description: ListingStore.upsert_listing writes a listing that already exists with INSERT OR REPLACE INTO listings. For an existing row, REPLACE resolves the conflict by deleting the existing row and inserting a new one. open_store sets PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON and migration 2 declares price_history.listing_id REFERENCES listings (id) ON DELETE CASCADE, so SQLite runs the cascade for that delete and removes every price_history row of the listing. The code then appends a history row only if the price changed: after a re-scrape with a changed price the history is just the new price, and after a re-scrape with an unchanged price, the common case, it is empty. No error, no warning. The method carries the previous id and first_seen_at into the REPLACE, so the id stays stable, which is what the existing tests check.
findings.evidence: Reproduction through the public API, on a new store: upsert_listing('kleinanzeigen', '1', price='100 €', currency='EUR', ...) at t0, then the same listing with price='90 €' at t0 + 1 h: price_history returns only the 9000 entry, the 10000 entry is gone. A third upsert with price='90 €' at t0 + 2 h: price_history returns [].
findings.impact: Every re-scrape of a known listing, the most frequent operation of the system, silently and irreversibly destroys its price history, which the search agents use to spot price drops.
findings.blocking_rationale: REQ-2 requires that no price history entry is lost except by an explicit delete. This loses it on the documented ingestion path, inside the operating envelope (one writer, the README's first example), and the loss cannot be undone once the launch has run.
findings.verification: After a first upsert, re-scrapes with changed and unchanged prices and a watcher update, price_history returns the first price followed by every later change, get_listing keeps the original id and first_seen_at, and delete_listing still removes the listing together with its history.

findings.title: Prices are stored one minor unit short on all three ingestion paths
findings.description: parse_amount returns the amount as a binary float (float(price) for numbers, float of the whole and fraction for text). Each ingestion path converts it with its own copy of int(amount * factor): upsert_listing in store.py, apply_update in updates.py and import_records in bulk.py. float('19.99') is 19.98999999999999843..., times 100 is 1998.9999999999998, and int() truncates it to 1998. About 4.6% of the amounts from 0.00 to 999.99 come out one minor unit short, always down, common retail prices among them: 19.99, 69.99, 17.99, 4.35, 8.20.
findings.evidence: upsert_listing('kleinanzeigen', '1', title='x', price='19,99 €', currency='EUR', ...) followed by get_listing(...)['price_minor'] gives 1998, not 1999. The same amounts come out short through apply_update and import_records.
findings.impact: Buyers are sent prices one minor unit below what the marketplace shows (19.98 € for an item priced 19.99 €), and a real change of one minor unit can vanish from the history.
findings.blocking_rationale: REQ-1 requires the exact number of minor units on all three paths, with '19,99 €' as its criterion's own example. The formats and amounts that fail are inside the operating envelope, and the buyers enrolled in the validation would see wrong prices.
findings.verification: '19,99 €', 19.99, '£17.99', '4,35 €' and '8.20' stored through upsert_listing, apply_update and import_records give price_minor 1999, 1999, 1799, 435 and 820, and amounts that land just above the integer in floating point ('1,10 €', '2.20', 0.55) are still exact.

body.justification: Two blocking findings: re-scrapes delete the price history, violating REQ-2 and realizing RISK-1, and prices are stored one minor unit short, violating REQ-1 and realizing RISK-2.
